objetivo.en: Describe a person: what they look like and what they are like.

nota.en: Alto for a man, alta for a woman.
The same for men and women.
Not “sympathetic”: simpático means nice or friendly.
The same for men and women.
Goes before the adjective and never changes.
Goes before the adjective and never changes.

explicacion.en: The adjective agrees with the person: alta for a woman, alto for a man.
To say what a person is like, use ser, not estar. English “is” does not tell you which verb to use.
Two women take the feminine plural: simpáticas. The masculine plural is only for men or a mixed group.

texto.en: The letter ñ, called eñe, is not the same as n. It sounds like the “ny” in “canyon”: señor is “seh-NYOR”, pequeño is “peh-KEH-nyo” and diseñador is “dee-seh-nya-DOR”. Do not say a plain n, and do not add an extra “ee”. Say it slowly: señor, pequeño, diseñador.

To say what a person is like, use ser + adjective: Daniela es alta. Mateo es simpático. In Spanish the adjective agrees with the person: it ends in -o for a man and in -a for a woman (alto, alta; simpático, simpática; divertido, divertida; delgado, delgada; tímido, tímida). For more than one person add -s: altos, altas. Adjectives that end in -e or in a consonant, like inteligente and joven, are the same for men and women: Emma es inteligente, Mateo es inteligente. Their plurals are inteligentes and jóvenes (joven adds -es and gets an accent mark in the plural). To make an adjective stronger, put muy (very) or bastante (quite) before it: Rosa es muy simpática. Muy and bastante never change. To ask what someone is like, say ¿Cómo es Daniela? Careful: ¿Cómo es...? asks what a person is like, while ¿Cómo está...? asks how that person is doing right now. For looks and personality, always use ser, never estar.
Adjectives agree with the person you describe. Tap each form to hear it.

objetivo.en: Describe a person's hair, eyes and clothes so others can recognize them.

nota.en: Singular in Spanish: el pelo, not “los pelos”.
For hair and clothes. For height, use bajo.
Lleva = he / she wears.
In Latin America: los lentes.
Always plural in Spanish.

explicacion.en: For hair and eyes use tener: tiene el pelo, tiene los ojos. Es is for what a person is like: es alto.
With parts of the body Spanish uses the, not “his” or “her”: tiene el pelo, tiene los ojos.
The color agrees with ojos, which is plural: marrón becomes marrones.
Lleva is for he or she. Llevo means I wear.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: b and v

texto.en: In Spanish, b and v are the same sound. There is no English “v” (with the teeth on the lip): both letters are a soft “b” made with the lips only. At the start of a word or after m or n, it is a firm “b”, like English b in “boy”: bien, bajo. Between vowels the lips barely touch: lleva, llevar, rubio. Say it slowly: lleva, llevar, rubio, bajo.

titulo.en: Hair, eyes and clothes: tener and llevar

texto.en: To describe the body, Spanish combines three verbs. Ser says what someone is like: Es alto. Tener says what someone has, such as hair and eyes: Tiene el pelo negro. Tiene los ojos azules. Notice el and los: Spanish says the hair, the eyes, not “his hair” or “her eyes”. The adjective agrees with pelo (masculine, singular) or with ojos (plural): el pelo largo, los ojos verdes. Llevar says what someone is wearing, such as clothes and glasses: Lleva una chaqueta azul. Lleva lentes. In Latin America, glasses are los lentes. The color goes after the noun and agrees with it: una camisa blanca, unos pantalones negros. Put it all together: Es alto, tiene el pelo corto y lleva una camisa blanca.

titulo.en: Colors agree with what they describe

titulo.en: Sound of the day: r and rr

texto.en: The letter r is called erre. A single r in the middle of a word is a quick tap of the tongue, like the “tt” in American “butter”: cerca, entre, detrás. At the start of a word, and when you write rr, the tongue vibrates: a strong trill, as in rojo and perro. The difference matters: pero means but, and perro means dog. Say it slowly: cerca, entre, detrás, rojo, perro.

titulo.en: Where is it? Prepositions of place, del and al

texto.en: To ask where a place is, say ¿Dónde está el banco? To answer, use está + a preposition of place: Está cerca de, lejos de, al lado de, enfrente de or detrás de + a place. Entre is different: it takes no de, and you name both places: entre el banco y el parque. Watch out for del and al. When de is followed by el, the two words always join into del: Está al lado del parque and never “de el parque”. When a is followed by el, they always join into al: Voy al mercado. English contractions are optional, but del and al are not. With la, los and las nothing changes: cerca de la tienda, de los parques, voy a la tienda. A full example: La farmacia está enfrente de la tienda y el banco está al lado de la farmacia.
With el, the words de and a join together. With la, los and las nothing changes. Tap each result to hear it.

objetivo.en: Ask whether there is something nearby and say where it is, telling hay and está apart.

explicacion.en: To say that something exists, use hay: Hay un banco. Está is for something you already know about.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: ll and y

texto.en: In most of Latin America, ll and y sound the same, like the y in English “yes”: calle, allí, yo. At the end of a word, y works as a vowel: hay sounds like English “eye”, and the word y, meaning and, sounds like the “ee” in “see”. Say it slowly: hay, calle, allí, yo.

Spanish has two ways to say “is / are” for places and things, and they do different jobs. Hay means “there is / there are”. It introduces something new, with un, una or no article at all: Hay un banco cerca. ¿Hay una farmacia? Sí, hay una. No, no hay. Hay never changes and is never used with el, la, los or las. Está, or están for several things, tells where something is when you already know which one: El banco está al lado del hotel. So ¿Hay un cajero? asks whether it exists, and ¿Dónde está el cajero? asks where it is. They often come one after the other: ¿Hay un cajero? Sí, el cajero está enfrente de la farmacia. Do not use es for this: English “is there” is hay.
Hay introduces something new. Está tells you where something you already know is. Tap each phrase to hear it.

explicacion.en: In the tú form, venir changes e to ie: vienes.
With yo the form is vengo, with a g. It is irregular.
The verb must match the person: ella viene, yo vengo.
Estar does not say where you are from. For “I'm from Chicago” use soy de Chicago (origin) or vengo de Chicago (where you come from).

titulo.en: Sound of the day: j and g

texto.en: The letter j, and g before e or i, sound like a strong English “h”, a little rougher than in “hat”: Loja, gente, Guadalajara. In Guadalajara the first g is before a, so it is a hard g like in “go”, and the j is the strong “h”. Say it slowly: Guadalajara, Loja, gente.

titulo.en: Venir de: where do you come from?

texto.en: Venir means to come. It is irregular. In the yo form it adds a g: vengo. In the tú, él / ella / usted and ustedes / ellos / ellas forms, the e changes to ie: vienes, viene, vienen. Venimos keeps its e. To ask where someone comes from, say ¿De dónde vienes? to a friend or ¿De dónde viene usted? to someone you address formally. To answer, use venir de + city or country: Vengo de Chicago. Mateo viene de Guadalajara. Venimos de Ecuador. Ser de and venir de are close but not identical. Soy de Chicago says where you are from, your origin; the usual question for that is ¿De dónde eres? Vengo de Chicago says the place you are coming from. When you meet someone from another city or country, ¿De dónde vienes? is also used to ask about where they come from, and that is how this lesson uses it. English “I'm from Chicago” is soy de or vengo de, never estoy de.
Vengo has a g. Vienes, viene and vienen change e to ie. Venimos keeps its e. Tap each form to hear it.
Places you will use in this lesson. Tap each one to hear it.
